overview: Amurdak people are connected with Country around Awunbarna, also called Mount Borradaile, in northwestern Arnhem Land. The map’s older label, Amarak, also appears in language catalogues. Rock paintings, oral histories and language records reveal artistic experimentation and relationships with neighbouring peoples and overseas visitors.

periods.title: New materials in an enduring painting tradition
periods.summary: Around the turn of the twentieth century, artists at Awunbarna experimented with laundry blue and elaborate hand figures. Research places this innovative phase broadly from the late nineteenth century into the 1960s.

periods.title: Knowledge holders and language records
periods.summary: Archived wordlists dated 1977 name Lucy Wirlmaga and Lily Marriyulgij as knowledge holders. Their contributions preserve evidence of Amurdak and its relationships with neighbouring languages.

periods.title: Traditional knowledge and collaborative research
periods.summary: The Art at a Crossroads project began in 2021 with senior Traditional Owner Charlie Mungulda collaborating in research on Awunbarna’s paintings and encounters with outsiders.

items.text: Awunbarna shelters contain grindstones, grinding hollows, shell middens, spears and wooden artifacts alongside introduced glass, metal and steel bed frames. The blue-painting study recorded these materials without excavating them. They bring food processing, equipment and changing household possessions into view, but do not supply a securely dated sequence for every object.

Amurdak oral and written histories describe trade, marriage and ceremonial relationships with neighbouring peoples. Encounters with British settlements, buffalo shooters and missionaries later altered those networks. This was a connected social landscape: neither imported goods nor contact-themed paintings demonstrate that earlier relationships simply vanished.

At the Major Art Site, AW22, artists used laundry blue in decorated hand paintings, including a hand placed over an earlier fish image. A material sold for whitening fabric became a strong ultramarine pigment. The sequence shows deliberate reuse of both a new material and an already painted surface.

Painted Hands combine a recognizable hand or hand-and-arm outline with added internal designs and sometimes a surrounding line. At Awunbarna they go beyond leaving a simple stencil. The 2020 study interprets their elaboration as a way of communicating identity and sustaining relationships during colonial upheaval, rather than proving one meaning for every hand.

A small horse painted across the border around an Awunbarna hand image provides a relative sequence: that horse was added after the border. Overlapping images, comparisons with documented works and recollections help researchers place paintings in time. Such evidence should not be turned into an exact calendar date for each image.

sections.title: Journeys and images of a changing world

items.text: Two paintings at inland Awunbarna depict boats that researchers identify as Moluccan fighting vessels. Their forms connect this rock-art landscape with seafaring worlds beyond Australia. The 2026 paper compares the images with historical evidence of Aboriginal voyages and longstanding Amurdak relationships with Iwaidja neighbours to the north.

Alamurdie, also known as Jack White, visited Tanimbar, Aru and Kei aboard a ship in 1839. Researchers propose that his experience could explain who made the boat paintings. This is an argued possibility, not a signed attribution or proof that every Amurdak person undertook such voyages.

Awunbarna’s large Rainbow Serpent paintings combine snake bodies with features of other creatures. Researchers distinguish recent examples through their upper positions in overlapping sequences, style and use of white clay pigment. White clay weathers differently from red ochre, so surviving colour and condition matter when interpreting the sequence.

The 2026 study proposes that making especially large ancestral figures helped reassert cultural authority amid the changes brought by European settlement. Size is directly observable; this explanation of its social purpose is the authors’ interpretation. A recent painting can therefore be innovative while remaining part of a much longer tradition.

AIATSIS lists a 1977 Amurdak wordlist with Lucy Wirlmaga as its knowledge holder and a comparison involving Amurdak, Garig and Iwaidja with Lily Marriyulgij. The catalogue restores named contributors to the history of language documentation. It describes records that can be located, rather than certifying that every word was independently checked for this card.

The educational guide for Language Matters identifies Charlie Mungulda’s Amurdak narration of the Warramurrungunji creation story. The recording preserves language used in an extended account, beyond a list of isolated words. The guide’s speaker information belongs to the documentary’s context and is not a present-day population census.

Mungulda appears as a coauthor of research on Amurdak encounters, bringing a songman’s knowledge into historical interpretation. The conference abstract describes a history built through oral accounts, rock paintings and documentary records. Community knowledge here participates in explaining the evidence, rather than serving only as an anonymous subject of study.

ending.text: There is no supported fall of an Amurdak kingdom to attach to this people’s history. Colonial encounters transformed life, and language transmission has faced severe loss. Amurdak knowledge nevertheless continues through custodianship, recordings and collaborative research. The map’s 1878 endpoint is a coverage limit, not evidence of disappearance.
